questions.q: What two matters still weighed on David the morning after he won his estate?
choices: Helping Alan escape, and the case of James of the Glens
Paying his uncle's debts, and mending the old house of Shaws
Finding a wife, and buying new horses for the estate
Writing to Mr. Campbell, and visiting his parents' graves
questions.evidence: I had still Alan, to whom I was so much beholden, on my hands

questions.q: What did Rankeillor say was David's clear duty to Alan?
choices: To help him out of the county, at any risk
To hand him over to the Lord Advocate
To send him straight back to Cluny's Cage at once
To keep him hidden at Shaws for a year
questions.evidence: I must help him out of the county at whatever risk

questions.q: Why did Rankeillor at first warn David against speaking up for James of the Glens?
choices: A great noble wanted vengeance, and David could be put on trial too
James was truly guilty, and David would only be telling a lie for him
The Lord Advocate had already set James free and needed no witnesses
David was too young for a court to listen to anything he had to say
questions.evidence: there is one way to shut your testimony out; and that is to put you in the dock

questions.q: What did Rankeillor do when David simply said he would "just have to be hanged"?
choices: Took back his advice and told David to go and do his duty
Laughed and said that David was talking like a foolish child
Grew angry and refused to write him any letters at all
Said he would go to the Lord Advocate in David's place
questions.evidence: Go and do your duty; and be hanged, if you must, like a gentleman

questions.q: What was the first of the two letters Rankeillor wrote for David?
choices: A letter to his bankers, placing a credit in David's name
A letter to Uncle Ebenezer, ordering him to leave Shaws
A letter to Mr. Campbell, telling him David was alive
A letter to an Appin lawyer, asking him to hire a ship
questions.evidence: is to my bankers, the British Linen Company, placing a credit to your name

questions.q: To whom was the second letter addressed?
choices: Mr. Balfour of Pilrig
Lord Advocate Grant himself
The Duke of Argyle
Captain Hoseason
questions.evidence: a letter to a namesake of your own, the learned Mr. Balfour of Pilrig

questions.q: As David left Shaws, a nightcap bobbed in a top window "like the head of a rabbit from a burrow." Who was it?
choices: Uncle Ebenezer
Torrance, the clerk
Mr. Rankeillor
A new servant
questions.evidence: the peak of a nightcap bobbing up and down

questions.q: How did David and Alan feel as they walked toward Edinburgh?
choices: Sad, because they knew they would soon part
Cheerful, because all their troubles were over
Nervous, because soldiers were close behind
Angry, because they had quarrelled again
questions.evidence: we were nearer tears than laughter

questions.q: What was the plan for getting Alan safely away?
choices: An Appin Stewart lawyer would find him a ship while Alan hid nearby
David would buy a horse so Alan could ride north to the Highlands
Rankeillor would hide Alan in his own house until the hunt was all over
Alan would walk to Queensferry and ask the lass to row him out
questions.evidence: it should be his part to find a ship and to arrange for Alan's safe embarkation

questions.q: Where did David and Alan say good-bye?
choices: Near Rest-and-be-Thankful
At the gates of Shaws
At the Hawes Inn door
On the castle hill in Edinburgh
questions.evidence: when we got near to the place called Rest-and-be-Thankful

questions.q: How did David feel after leaving Alan and walking down into the city?
choices: So lost and lonesome he could have sat and cried
Free at last, and glad to be done with outlaws
Excited to spend his money in the shops
Afraid that Alan would be caught by soldiers that day
questions.evidence: I felt so lost and lonesome

questions.q: What is this last chapter mostly about?
choices: David plans his next duties and sadly parts from Alan
David and Alan sail away together to begin new lives in France
David moves into the House of Shaws and sends his uncle away
Alan is captured by soldiers on the road into Edinburgh
questions.evidence: we had come to where our ways parted
